en: Now, this *Śabdabhedaprakāśa* (The Illumination of Lexical Variants), having assumed a form [as a treatise], has been composed by me for the sake of awakening those unlearned in grammar, even while seeking the favor of virtuous poets; it is an illumination of the lexical variants within the entire ocean of speech.
(1) Generally, that usage which is abundant and recognized through authoritative examples shall be employed.
Among the various distinct forms and other qualities that differ in their characteristics, the wise person should determine that very [reality]. || 2 ||
In some cases here, the distinction is made by the prosodic measure (mātrā), in some by the phoneme (varṇa);
in some it arises from the indication of a different meaning, and in some from the conventional usage of words.

He whose mind remains awake within the lotus of his heart is the master of the manifestation of words and their meanings; he possesses the freedom to employ them at will, while remaining locked against the intrusion of others' applications.
One should know that *vidyāt* [is used for] *agāra* and *āgāra*, as well as *apaga* and *āpagā*. Furthermore, *arāti* and *ārāti* are mentioned, as are *ama* and *āma*. (5)
*Amarṣa* may be *āmarṣa*, and *aṅkura* as well as *aṅkūra*;
*antarikṣa* as *antarīkṣa*, and *agastya* as *agasti*;
*aṭarūpa* as *āṭarūṣa*, and *avaśya* as *avaśyāya*. (6)
Pratiśyāya, pratiśyāva, bhālūka, and also bhalluka;
they call it jambūka and jambūka, as well as śambūka and śambuka. (7)
Jatukā may be jatūkā, and masura may be like masūra;
likewise, vāstuka may be vāstūka, and devakī may be daivakī.
Jyotiṣam and jyautiṣam, as well as ṣṭhevanam and ṣṭhīvanam; likewise sutrāmā and sūtrāmā, and hanūmān and hanumān.
*Uṣaṇam* and *ūṣaṇam* mean pungent; *ūṣaram* and *ūṣaram* mean saline soil.
*Hārītaḥ* and *hāritaḥ* may refer to both a sage and a specific bird. (10)
*Tuvaram* and *stūvaram* would mean "quickly," while *kuvaraḥ* and *kūvare* mean "crooked.
*Anuttamam* means "supreme," and *āhatam* would mean "struck" or "beaten," whereas *anāhatam* means "unstruck" or "unbeaten. || 11 ||
One may be *anudāra* (not noble) despite being *udāra* (noble); likewise, one may appear *anudagravat* (as if not lofty) even when *udagra* (lofty).
*Bandhūram* and *bandhuram* both mean beautiful; *ūrīkṛtam* and *urīkṛtam* both mean accepted or undertaken.
Vālhīka and Vālhika, Gāṇḍīva and also Gāṇḍiva;
Uṣā and Ūṣā, Nanandā and also Nanāndā are thus proclaimed.
*Hrīvera* is *hirivera*, and *cikūra* is also *cikura*;
likewise, *caṇḍāla* is *caṇḍāla*, and *vadanya* is like *vadānya*. (14)
They call it *hālāhala*, *hālahala*, and also *halāhala*; they likewise designate it as *ḍāhāla*, *ḍahāla*, and *ḍāhala*. (15)
Koṅkāṇa and Koṅkaṇa, Śyāmāka and Śyāmaka;
Sahācara and Sahacara, as well as Sphaṭika and Sfāṭika. || 16 ||
Gandharva and gāndharva; camara and cāmara; cora and caura; caṭu and cāṭu; cela and caila; camu and camū. || 17 ||
*Cañcu* and *cañcūsta* mean the palm of the hand; *śyāmala* and *śāmala* mean dark-complexioned;
*mahilā* and *mahelelā* are among the words for woman; and *vidagdha* and *che kilo* mean clever. (18)
The word *guggulu* may be used for *guggulu*, and *hiṅgula* for *hiṅgula*;
likewise, *mandira* may be used for *mandira*, and *vīryā* is also said to denote *vīrya*. (19)
Dhanyāka is also dhānyāka; yutaka is yautaka, as it is; kavāṭa is kapāṭa, and kavila is considered to be kapila. || 20 ||
*Karavāla* and *karapāla* [mean sword]; *vanīyaka* and *vanīpaka* [mean beggar]; *pārāvata* and *pārapata* [mean pigeon]; and *javā* occurs together with *japayā*. (21)
Jaṭāyuṣā becomes Jaṭāyu, and likewise Vidyādāyuṁ becomes Āyuṣā;
sāyaṁ becomes sāyaḥ, koṣaḥ becomes kośaḥ, and śaṇdaḥ becomes śaṇḍavat.
*Taviṣam* and *taviṣam*, as well as *musalaḥ* and *muśalaḥ*; *veśaḥ* and *veṣaḥ* are said to be synonymous; likewise, *husaḥ* and *buṣaḥ*. (23)
One who knows the bow may be called *tanuṣā* along with *tanu*, and *dhanuṣā* along with *dhanus*.
A boar may be called *sūkara* as well as *sūkaraḥ*, and a jackal likewise *sṛgāla* as well as *sṛgālavat*.
Sūra and Śūra, taraṇi and kalasa as well as kalaśa;
Sunāsīra and Śunāśīra, and Nārāyaṇa and Narāyaṇa. (25)
Jāmbavān may also be Jāmbava, and Lakṣmaṇa may also be Lakṣaṇa;
likewise, saṃstara may be srastara, and caritra may be carita.
Pārataṃ and pāradaṃ; vāsraḥ and vāsaraḥ; kṛmiḥ like kṛmiḥ; tṛphalā and trifalā; and also tṛṇatā and triṇatā. || 27 ||
*Bhaved* would be *dṛṣṭiḥ*, and likewise *riṣṭiḥ*; *priyālaḥ* would be like *piyālaḥ*. *Kaṇāṭīnaḥ* would be *kalāṭīnaḥ*, and also *vātikaḥ* would be *vātigaḥ*. (28)
They know *mihiro* and *mahiro*, as well as *mukuro* and *makuro*; likewise, they recognize *mukulaṃ* and *makulaṃ*, and *mukuṭaṃ* and *makuṭaṃ*. (29)
*Mukuti* and *makuti*, as well as *caluka* and *culuka*; *karañja* and *karaja* may likewise be used; and *pareta* is considered synonymous with *pretavan*. (30)
*Kirmira* and *kirmora*, *hāyana* and *hāyana* are synonymous; likewise, *śauṭīrya* and *śauṭīra*, and *jyaiṣṭha* and *jyeṣṭha* are seen to be interchangeable. (31)
The word *vāna* may mean dryness or wind, while *udaka* is considered to mean water.
*Śatarūṣī* and *śatārū* are both declared to be names for a particular variety of *kuṣṭha*.
The Dreṣkāṇa-dreṣkāṇas and Dṛkkāṇa-dṛkkāṇas are also like the [original] Dreṣkāṇas and Dṛkkāṇas; likewise, the Patraṅga is like the Patraṅga, and the Kuddāla is like the Kuddāla. (33)
*Māriṣa* and *mārūṣa* refer to the *śāka* plant; *plīhā* also refers to the disease of the spleen (*plīharoga*).
*Felī* and *feli* likewise refer to what is left over (*ucchiṣṭa*); and *kākinī* refers to a *kākiṇī*. || 34 ||
Saudāmanī, saudāmnī, and saudāminī are also accepted [as synonyms for lightning]. Jaraṭha may also be jaṭhara, and nimeṣa may also be nimiṣa. || 35 ||
Buka and baka are names for a flower; madana and mavana for a tree;
and āragvadha and āragavatha, as well as khuraka and kṣuraka, [are synonyms]. (36)
Vṛṣṇi and Pṛśni are both called Sarayu and Sarayū;
Nīlaṅgu is also called Nīlāṅgurīśvarī and Īśvarā. (37)
*Tāpiñcha* is also *tāpiccha*, and *tripuṣa* as well as *trapuṣa*;
likewise, *ḍiṇḍīra* is also *hiṇḍīra*, and *paraśu* together with *parśu*.
*Bālikā*, *bālukā*, *dordoṣa*, *bhuja*, *bhuj*, *bāhu*, and *bāhā* denote the arm; *tviṣ* and *tviṭ* denote luster; and *sandhyā* is likewise used for the junction (of day and night). || 39 ||
They know *bhaginīm* as "sister" and *bhagnīm* as "broken"; likewise, they know *zhillarīm* and *zhallarīm*; and they say *retam* along with *retasā*, as well as *edham* with *edhasā*. (40)
*Saṃvanana* and *saṃvadana*, as well as *taruṇī* and *talunī*, and *pramadāvana* and *pramadavana* are thus proclaimed. (41)
*Khārulī* would be *khuralī*; likewise, *vajra* and *vajrāśani*.
*Śilam-uñcham*, *śiloñcham*, and also *uñchaśilam* would be [synonymous]. (42)
Dharitrī and Dhārayitrī, as well as Mahiṣī and Māhiṣī; Vāsudeva may also be called Vāsu, and Vāmadeva likewise Vāmavat.

*Lakṣmī* and *lakṣī* refer to the goddess Lakṣmī; *hari* refers to the wife of Hari (Lakṣmī). *Rūvaka* and *rūvakaḥ* are said to mean "a small coin," and *urūvūka* is also used in that same sense. (44)
*Kumuda* may be used with *kumudā*, and *yoṣit* with *yoṣitā*;
likewise, *śarat* may be used with *śaradā*, and *prāvṛṭ* with *prāvṛṣā*. (45)
He is the sky together with the sky, austerity together with austerity, patience together with patience, and greatness together with greatness in splendor.
Darkness is said to arise from darkness, and passion likewise from passion;
and by the grammarians, they are called *jalaukas* because they are like water-creatures (*jalaukā*). (47)
*Divam* is said to be equivalent to *divā*, as is *parṣat* with *pariṣad*;
*varṣāḥ* may be used for *variṣābhiḥ*, and *harṣaḥ* also for *hariṣeṇa*. (48)
*Sarṣapa* and *sariṣapa*, as well as *karṣa* and *kariṣeṇa*;
*mārṣa* and *māriṣa* are thus stated, just as *sparśa* is also [spelled] *spariśa*. (49)

In this way, other [consonants] such as *v* and *r*, as well as the sibilants (*ūṣman*), may optionally be placed on the *mūrdhan* (the *upadhmānīya*) through usage, due to the fear of violating the metrical structure of the *chandas* and so forth. (50)
They know that fasting is generally practiced only toward the south;
one who knows the arts should be skilled in the *kalās* according to the power of the meter and the intention.
It is taught that the meaning of a collective group (samūha) and that which is born (jāta) belong to the *ca*-class [consonants];
however, the state of being a semi-vowel (*antasthīya*) and the letter *ya* are said to belong to the grass (*yavasa*). 52.
Even in the weaving of a weaver, the state of being the warp and so forth is observed;
likewise, the wise declare that *rīrbārū* beginning with the fourth vowel (*ū*) refers to the *karkaṭī* fruit. (53)
The word *arti* is accepted as having a short vowel when meaning "affliction" or "pain," and also when referring to the tip of a bow.
These two [forms] belong to the middle and the *tavarga* (dental) groups respectively, and they possess the power of the lapis lazuli gem (*vaidūrya-maṇi*). 54.
The letter *ra* is in the middle of the *tavarga*; *niṣadvara* means "at night" and "in the mud";
*dhmāna* preceded by *ut-* refers to the hearth; and *dhāna* and *hāna* are also mentioned. 55.

The word *yavānī* has its middle syllable palatal (*tālavya*), is clear, contains the word *ūrdhva*, and possesses the letter *v*; it has *vam* in the middle. In the month of Śrāvaṇa, the middle [day] is the *madhyava*.
In the word *śaure*, the letter *k* belongs to the *ka*-group; and in the word *kṣuraprake*, which refers to the barber’s tool, the conjunction with the letter *ṣ* (*kaṣa-saṃyoga*) is intended. (57)
They call Avyayānavyaya Doṣāśabda at night; Kanyākubja is Kānyakubja, and Kośala is Uttarakośalā.
It is called Vārāṇasī, and likewise Vāṇārasī;
Tāmaliptā and Dāmaliptā; Taṅka and also Ataṅka. (59)
Nandī and nandi, as well as patrī and pattri, are synonyms; vasnasā and snasā refer to a tendon.
Yamalam and yāmalam denote a pair or couple; khaṇḍila and khaṇṭiḍa are equivalent terms for a small plot of land.
Janitrī and janayitrī, kafoṇi and kaphaṇi;
likewise, vālmika and vālmīka, and bālī is also said to be bāli. (61)
*Kusuma* with *sumena*, *maranda* with *makarandavat*, and *ahituṇḍika*—these are said to become *āhituṇḍika*. (62)
Vidyādaṇḍī is Rāmaṇḍīra-maṇi; furthermore, āṇivat is āmaṇḍa.
Maṇḍā is veraṇḍa, and asana is also used for priyakaṭha. || 63 ||
Apiśali is used in the sense of a sage, as is Āpiśali;
Candrabhāgā and Candrabhāgī are synonyms, and Khani is also recorded as a name for a mine.
*Gonāsa* and *gonasa* both mean "serpent"; *phālguna* and *phalguna* refer to Arjuna.
When the thumb is joined with the index finger, it is called *prādeśa*, which is like a *pradeśa* (a measure). || 65 ||
For an elephant, the words *gaja*, *mataṅga*, and *mātaṅga* are used; for a serpent, *nāga*, *kālīyaka*, and *kāliya*;
for the *rohītaka* tree, *rohitaka* is also used; and *ūṣara* is considered a synonym for *muṣara*.
*iṣīkā* may be *īṣīkā*; likewise, *vānāyuja* and *javanāyuja*.
*Guvāka* and *gūvāka* both refer to the betel nut; *kuc* and *kūca* denote the breast. (67)
*Kukara* is the same as *kuṇi*, *kūṇi*, *nāka*, *kulaka*, and *kūlaka*. *Paugaṇḍa* is the same as *apogaṇḍa*; *ulūta* is the same as *alūta*. (68)
*Kākācika* may be *kākacika*, and it should be seen as being like *ṛṣya*;
*vātūla* may also be *vātula*, and *kaikeyī* may also be *kekayī*. (69)
Viriñci, virañci, and viriñcana refer to Brahmā;
varūda and vārūda mean one who has descended; and vikka and pikka denote a young elephant.
*Karkareṭu* and *kareṭu* are synonyms for *kurkura* and *kukkura* (dog); likewise, *ambarīṣa* and *ambarīṣa* are synonyms. *Kuvala* and *kuva* refer to the blue lotus (*utpala*). || 71 ||
*Kumārila* and *kumāri* refer to the churning-stick and the act of churning; *mathi* and *manthau* also mean the churning-stick.
*Vajrā*, *vajrī*, *snuhī*, and *bhārgī* are names for the Euphorbia plant; *varalā* and *varaṭā* are also [names for that same plant]. || 72 ||
*Kaiṭabha* and *kaiṭabhīśvarī*, *kandarya* and *kandarā*, as well as *bhidir* and *bheda*; *kuliśa* [denotes] the thunderbolt, *vāti* [denotes] the wind, and *kuṭiḥ* [denotes] a hut. (73)
*Kari* may mean "elephant" or "hair"; *jaṭi* occurs in the sense of "matted hair," and *śilā* also means "rock.
*Pulinda* refers to a forest-dweller, as does *pulindra*; likewise, *niṣāda* applies to both a man and a woman of that caste. (74)

A *yati* is said to be *yatini*; *sṛkviṇī*, *sṛkvi*, and *sṛkva* refer to the corners of the mouth; *vahitam* and *vahitram* mean a boat; and *nicula*, *hijjala*, and *ijjala* denote the water-hyssop plant.
Vikhu, vikha, and vigra [are so called] because of the disappearance of the nose;
likewise, amati and amati [refer to] time, and tamas and tamī [refer to] the night. (76)
*Viśvapsan* and *viśvapsā*, as well as *sidhma* and *sidhmā*, are so described; *dhṛk* is used together with *bukkayā*, and *dharma* and *dharmam* are also proclaimed [as synonyms]. || 77 ||
Heat (ūṣman) is said to be together with heat (ūṣmā), and marrow (majjā) is said to be together with marrow (majjā);
likewise, the penis (śeṣa) and the scrotum (śepa) are together with the penis (śeva), and the penis (śepa) is declared to be together with the penis (śepas).
They say *prāpuṇṇāṭaka* and *prapunnāṭa* refer to the *prapunnāṭa* plant;
likewise, *araraṃ* and *ārari* are used for a door-panel, just like *kapāṭa*.
The words *bhallo* and *bhalli* may refer to an arrow or a leaf; *pātram* and *patravat* mean a vessel or a leaf.
*Īrma* and *īrmā* may denote a wound, while *jharaḥ* and *jhariḥ* may signify a waterfall or a stream.

If there is *āmātya* [fever], it may occur even in an *amātya* [minister]; if there is *pīnasa* [nasal catarrh], there may be *apīnasa*. An *anvāsana* [enema] is prescribed, and likewise an *anuvāsana* [oil enema] should be administered. (81)
The word *yūṣa* (soup) and *yabhana* (copulation) should go to the letter *ya*, as they are considered non-dual from it;
likewise, *parūṣa* (a thorn) and *parūḥ* (a knot), as well as *kāśmīrī* and *kāsmirī* (the saffron plant). 82.
The word *mātuluṅga* is used for the citron fruit (*mātuliṅga*), and *kadala* is likewise used for the plantain tree (*kadala*).
The term *parūṣaka* is said to refer to the fruit, while *purūṣa* and *parūṣa* are used in the same sense. (83)
The word *nāgaraṅga* may also refer to an orange; likewise, *visaṇḍaka* refers to a lotus stalk (*vise*).
Furthermore, the term *vārtāku* is used for eggplant (*vārtāka*), and the form *vṛntāka* is also observed. (84)
*Kisala* refers to a sprout; *guccha* is like a cluster (*guluñcha*).
*Amlāta* may be used for the *amlātaka* flower, as well as *amlātakam*. || 85 ||
*Jambīra* is also *jāmbīra*; for *jūrṇā*, there is also *jūrṇi*. For *tittira*, there is also *tittira*; and for *pipīlaka*, there is *pīlaka*.
*Godā* refers to the river Godāvarī; *madhurā* refers to the city of Mathurā;
*kavika* refers to the bird *kavikā*; and *gavedha* refers to the plant *gavedhukā*. (87)
For a chest, the words *mañjūṣā*, *piṭaka*, *peṭā*, and *peṭaka* are used.
For an infantryman, the terms *pādāta*, *padāti*, *pādāta*, and *padātika* are employed. (88)
A *pannadhrī* is applied even to a sandal;
a *jalāyukā* is for a leech; and a *gaverūka* is for red ochre. (89)
A crocodile (*nakra*) is [found] in the nose, and a crooked one (*vaṅka*) is also said to be in the mouth;
*saraṇī* is in the extension, and *phalaka* or *phala* is in the scrotum.
The word *dāda* may also mean "fang," and *śalmalī* refers to the silk-cotton tree (*śālmali*).
Furthermore, *bandhukā* can mean "bride," and *aṅganā* may also refer to the *añjanī* plant. (91)
The *alābu* (gourd) ends in a short vowel, yet it is understood as beginning with a long one;
the *ūrṇanābha* (spider) ends in a short *i*, while the *kikīdivi* (blue jay) appears both as *kikīdive* and *kikīdivi*.
*Kareṭu* and *karaṭu* are also used for a messenger; likewise, *dūtī* is recorded as a term for a female messenger.
*Nicola* is synonymous with *niculaka*, and *asiknī* is synonymous with *asiknikā*.
Jīvañjīva is used for the jīvañjīva bird, and cālana for the cālanī sieve; likewise, syūna is used for what is sewn (syūta), and syona as well as abhyuṣa for the abhyuṣa plant. || 94 ||
*Karamba* refers to a mixture; *vānta* means vomited; *bhānta* refers to curd mixed with parched barley flour (*dadhisaktu*).
*Āmikṣā* is also written with a short vowel in the middle (*āmikṣā*), and *yautaka* has the syllable *ka* in the middle (*yautaka*). || 95 ||

*Dhuvitra* and *nirūkāra* are synonyms for a winnowing fan; likewise, *ṛṣau* and *riṣiḥ* refer to a sage. *Iriṇam* (with a long vowel) denotes a barren spot, as does *kṛṣakaḥ* and *kṛṣikaḥ*, which refer to a farmer. || 96 ||

When [the sounds] *sarvalā* and *sarvalī* are spoken with the palatal (*tālavya*) and dental (*dantya*) [articulations respectively], this [deity] is intended as Āśuśukṣaṇi, whose middle consists of two palatals. (97)
The word *dāśārha* is considered to have its middle *r* sound as a palatal (*tālavya*) when referring to Viṣṇu;
however, it has a final palatal *r* when it means "lord of ten million. The word *prāś* has both palatal and dental *r* sounds. (98)
The letter *da* with the dental *u* (du) refers to cotton (*karpāsa*) and that which is soiled by food;
it is also said to refer to sour gruel (*kāñjika*) and boiled rice with water (*kulmāṣa*). 99.
The *ādidantya* (initial-toothed) consists of *suṣavī*, *sambākṛta*, and *samūru*; while *kusīda* and *kusūla* are declared to be *madhyadantya* (middle-toothed). 100.
The word *pārāvāraḥ* has *pa* in the middle; *sopānam* begins with a dental (*da*). *Viśvastā* has *va* in the middle and is not cited as *viśastā*. (101)
The syllables beginning with the second letter of the *ka*-group and ending with *kṣa* may also be used as *khullaka*;
likewise, those beginning with the second letter of the *pa*-group, as well as *pha* and *ṭa*, are used in the sense of "hood" (*phaṇā*).

That which begins with the thirteenth vowel is declared to be *śobhāñjana*; it ends with the letter *ta* belonging to the root *tanūnapāt*, and does not possess the third letter of the dental class (*tavarga*).

Furthermore, the fifth letter of the dental class (na) followed by the penultimate letter (ma), standing alone as *maṅgana*, and the word *hāhā* ending with an *s* (*hāhās*), are said to be the names of the celestial singers (*divyagāyan*). 104.

They know that the middle of the *ca*-group [the letter *ja*] in a four-hall structure is a *sañjavana*; and the letter *ra*, which is the end of the *pa*-group [the letter *ma*], signifies an inferior purpose. (105)
Antasthamadhya, vaiyātya, vemni, vema, and vemaka;
kamana and kāmana; and kūkuda is remembered as beginning with a long vowel. || 106 ||
The word *bhās* meaning "light" also ends in a final *s* and is exclusively masculine;
likewise, one who is not mute is called *aneḍamūka*, and the word *śūrmī* is also recorded as *śūrmis*.
The word *eḍūka* may have a short middle vowel or a short final vowel; it is also used as a compound ending in a vowel.
Furthermore, for the word *śaibala*, there are the forms *śaibāla*, *śebala*, and *śībala*. (108)

*Tūṇa* and *tūṇī* mean a quiver; *tūṇīra* also means a quiver. *Marīca* and *marica* both mean black pepper. *Citra* and *citraka* may mean variegated or a leopard. *Cintiyā* also refers to anxiety or thought. || 109 ||
In the Veda, there is *anaḍvāhī*; in common speech (*bhāṣā*), there is also *anaḍuhī*.
There is also a flattened *madhyakāra* (the letter *ka* in the middle); *uraṇa* occurs with the short vowel *u* and others, as well as with *ava*.
They say that *ikārādi* refers to an excellent cow, while *naicikī* refers to a reddish-brown cow;
*sāci* is used in the sense of "crookedly," and likewise *astathā* is used in the sense of "as it actually is."
The letter *ya* is also said to denote the first of the labial class (*cavarga*), as well as a sister and the wife of one's own clan;

*Laṅgūlam* is also *lāṅgūlam*; *bhambharā* is also *bhambharālī*.
*Tvaci* may be *tvacaḥ*, and *kiro* may be *kiraḥ*; likewise, *pathaḥ* is used for *pathi*. (116)
Ajagāva, ājagāvam, and likewise ājigavam; ajagavam is used for the Pināka bow, and tamastamāḥ for the son of Siṃhikā (Rāhu).

The words *agādha*, *asthāgha*, *asthāga*, and *asthāyam* are employed in the sense of that which is unfathomable.
The word *madhya* may denote the middle heat and likewise the fourth [heat] of sin;

*Draviḍa* may mean "madhya" (middle) as well as *kāphala*; *kaṭphala* [is another term].

The word *ulūka* has a short vowel in the middle, and *alimpaka* begins with a short vowel;
likewise, in the word *kuruvaka*, the letter *r* is employed without the vowel *u*.

Regarding the word *mañjiṣṭhā*, however, *bhaṇḍīrī* is also taught as having a middle short vowel; it may also begin with a long vowel. Furthermore, the word for a scorpion (*vṛścika*) may be *alī*, and it may also be *ālī*. (122)
*Bukka* and *bukkā* mean memory; *bukkin* refers to a neck-ornament. *Khoḍa* and *khora* denote one who is lame. *Tarī* and *taris* are also [synonyms for a boat]. 123.
Nasya is for the nose; manthāna is also for me (the churner).
Kārtasvara has a medial *d* sound; sīhuṇḍa is like sīhuṇḍa.
The word *lulāya* (buffalo) begins and ends with a labial; it also possesses the status of having a final consonant (*halanta*) when joined with the wind (*marut*).
One should know that in the word *purūravas*, there is also lengthening of the letter *ū*.
*Kurūṇṭha* may also begin with a long vowel; it is likewise accepted as *sairēya*.
*Nālikera* may end in a short *i*, as well as having a long vowel as its second syllable. (126)

The word *kāṇḍa* is used for an arrow and for excellence; *śaru* is used for peace and for variegated arrows; and both *kiṃśuka* and *śuka* are recorded as being pronounced with either palatal (*tālavya*) or dental (*dantya*) *ś*. (127)
The words *śūnā*, *suṅga*, and *suraṅgā* belong to both the dental and palatal classes;
*koṭīśa* is also [palatal], while *ribhukṣa* is non-dental, meaning both "heaven" and "vajra. (128)

The Kinnara and the horse-faced [being] are both distinct and non-distinct, like the Daityas and Asuras; likewise, *riṣṭa* and *ariṣṭa* have a non-distinct meaning in some views, while in others they have a distinct meaning. (129)

In the case of non-essential derivative words such as *vāgmī* (eloquent), *vālmīki* (born from a termite hill), *ulkā* (firebrand), *satra* (sacrificial session), *chatra* (umbrella), and *patatrī* (bird)—which denote those who possess or are associated with these things—the suffix *ini* is not employed. The lord of poets, Maheśvara—who has gazed across the ocean of all medical doctrines to its very depths and is a sun to the cluster of lotuses in the waters of the scriptures of grammar—has composed this work with great effort; let it be examined at will by the virtuous, for it is beyond price.

This composition consists of the rules for words and phonemes as they are conceptualized through the *Nāmapārāyaṇa*, the *Oṇādi* lists, and the *Nirukta*, and it is indeed approved by the learned. (47)
